title: Secrets & configuration management
summary: Keep API keys out of your code, load settings from the environment, and never commit a secret to Git again.
objectives: Explain why secrets must never live in source code or Git history
Separate configuration from code using environment variables
Load secrets safely with a .env file and python-dotenv
Protect secrets with .gitignore and an .env.example template
Call the Anthropic Claude API using a key read from the environment
Know how secrets are injected in CI/CD and cloud deployments
Respond correctly when a secret leaks

quiz.q: Where should an API key like ANTHROPIC_API_KEY live?
options: In an environment variable, loaded at runtime
In the README so teammates can find it
Committed to Git in a config.py
quiz.why: Secrets belong in the environment (or a secret manager), never in source code. Code reads them at runtime via os.environ.

quiz.q: Why must the .env file be added to .gitignore?
quiz.answer: So it is never committed to Git, keeping real secrets out of the repository and its history.
quiz.why: Once a secret is pushed to a shared or public repo it is considered compromised, even after deletion, because it stays in history.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of an .env.example file?
options: It stores the real production keys
It is a committed template listing variable names with no real values
quiz.why: .env.example is committed and documents which variables are needed, using placeholder values so teammates know what to set.

quiz.q: True or false — deleting a leaked key from a file and committing the fix makes the repo safe.
quiz.why: False. The key remains in Git history. You must rotate (revoke and regenerate) the key, not just delete it.

quiz.q: In Python, how do you read an environment variable named ANTHROPIC_API_KEY?
quiz.why: The os module exposes the environment; getenv returns None (or a default) if the variable is missing instead of raising.

quiz.q: How are secrets provided to a deployed app or a CI/CD pipeline?
options: You commit the .env file to the deploy branch
Through the platform's secret store or repository secrets, injected as env vars
You email them to the server
You paste them into the build log
quiz.why: Platforms like GitHub Actions and cloud hosts provide encrypted secret stores that are injected as environment variables at run time.

body_markdown:
## Why secrets must leave your code

A **secret** is any value that grants access: an API key, a database password, a token. The golden rule is simple — secrets never belong in source code. If you hard-code a key, anyone who reads your repo can use it, and once it is pushed to Git it lives in the **history** forever, even after you delete the line.

This matters for your portfolio. Public GitHub repos are scanned constantly by bots, and a leaked Anthropic or cloud key can be abused within minutes, running up a bill on your account.

## Configuration belongs in the environment

The fix is to separate **configuration** from **code**. Your code stays the same everywhere; only the settings change between your laptop, a teammate's machine, and production. The standard place to put those settings is **environment variables** — named values the operating system hands to your program at run time.

```python
import os

api_key = os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"]   # raises if missing
debug = os.getenv("DEBUG", "false")          # default if missing
```

Use `os.environ[...]` when the value is required, and `os.getenv(name, default)` when it is optional.

## The .env file for local development

Typing `export VAR=...` every session is tedious, so locally we keep settings in a **.env** file and load them with **python-dotenv**. The `.env` file is for your machine only — it must never be committed.

```bash
# .env  (NEVER commit this file)
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-your-real-key-here
DEBUG=true
```

```python
from dotenv import load_dotenv
import os

load_dotenv()                                # reads .env into the environment
key = os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"]
```

## Protect it with .gitignore and a template

Two files keep you safe. Add `.env` to **.gitignore** so Git ignores it, and commit an **.env.example** with the variable *names* but fake values, so teammates know what to set.

```bash
# .gitignore
.env
.env.*
!.env.example
```

The `.env.example` is committed; the real `.env` is not.

## Using a secret with the Claude API

The Anthropic client reads `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` from the environment automatically — you never pass the key in code.

```python
from dotenv import load_dotenv
from anthropic import Anthropic

load_dotenv()
client = Anthropic()                         # picks up ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)
```

## Secrets in CI/CD and the cloud

Your `.env` never leaves your laptop, so how does a deployed app get its keys? Through the platform's encrypted **secret store**. In GitHub Actions you add **repository secrets** and reference them in the workflow; the host injects them as environment variables at run time.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
steps:
  - run: python app.py
    env:
      ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
```

If a key ever leaks, **rotate** it — revoke the old one and generate a new one. Deleting the file is not enough.

slides.title: Secrets & configuration management
slides.narration: Welcome to Month Four, where we build real portfolio projects. In this lesson we tackle something every professional gets right and every beginner gets wrong at least once: managing secrets and configuration. By the end you'll keep your A P I keys safe, load settings from the environment, and never commit a secret to Git again.

slides.title: What is a secret?
bullets: Never belongs in your source code.
slides.narration: First, what do we mean by a secret? It's any value that grants access: an A P I key, a database password, an access token. The rule is simple. Secrets never belong in your source code. A leaked Anthropic key can be abused within minutes, running up a real bill on your account.

slides.title: Git remembers everything
bullets: Pushed secrets live in history forever.
Public repos are scanned by bots.
Deleting the line does not remove it.
Once leaked, treat it as compromised.
slides.narration: Here's the dangerous part. Git remembers everything. If you push a key and then delete that line in a later commit, the key still sits in your history where anyone can find it. Bots scan public repos constantly. So once a secret is pushed, you must treat it as compromised, full stop.

slides.title: Config in the environment
slides.code:
import os

key = os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"]
debug = os.getenv("DEBUG", "false")
slides.narration: The fix is to separate configuration from code. Your program stays identical on your laptop and in production; only the settings change. We put those settings in environment variables, which the operating system hands to your program at run time. Use os dot environ when a value is required, and os dot getenv with a default when it's optional.

slides.title: The .env file
slides.narration: Typing export commands every session is tedious, so locally we keep settings in a dot env file. It's just lines of key equals value. The python dotenv library reads this file into your environment. Remember, this file is for your machine only and must never be committed to Git.

slides.title: Load it in Python
bullets: Then read from os.environ as normal.
Works the same in dev and prod.
slides.code:
from dotenv import load_dotenv
import os

load_dotenv()
key = os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"]
slides.narration: Loading it is two lines. Import load dotenv and call it at the top of your program. It reads the dot env file into the environment. After that you read your variables with os dot environ exactly as before. The beauty is your code is identical whether the values come from a dot env file or from a real production environment.

slides.title: Gitignore and a template
slides.narration: Two files keep you safe. Add dot env to your gitignore so Git never tracks it. Then commit a file called dot env dot example, with the variable names but fake placeholder values. That template documents what teammates need to set, without ever exposing a real secret.

slides.title: Claude API reads it for you
bullets: You never pass the key in code.
slides.code:
from anthropic import Anthropic
client = Anthropic()
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role":"user","content":"Hi"}])
slides.narration: Good libraries make this easy. The Anthropic client automatically reads ANTHROPIC underscore A P I underscore KEY from the environment, so you never write the key in your code. You just create the client and call messages dot create with your model and messages. The key flows in silently from the environment.

slides.title: Secrets in CI/CD
bullets: Injected as env vars at run time.
slides.narration: Your dot env never leaves your laptop, so how does a deployed app get its keys? Through the platform's encrypted secret store. In GitHub Actions you add repository secrets, then reference them in your workflow Yaml like this. The host injects them as environment variables when your job runs. Same pattern, just managed by the platform.

slides.title: When a secret leaks
bullets: Deleting the file is not enough.
slides.narration: Mistakes happen, so know the drill. If a key ever leaks, you rotate it. That means revoke the old key in the provider's dashboard and generate a fresh one. Deleting the file does nothing, because the old key still works and still lives in history. Update the new key everywhere it's used, then investigate how it leaked.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: Secrets never go in code or Git.
Task: move your keys into a .env file.
slides.narration: Let's recap. Secrets never go in your code or Git history. Configuration lives in environment variables. Locally you use a dot env file, ignore it with gitignore, and commit a dot env dot example template. In the cloud, the platform's secret store does the same job. Your task before the next lesson: take a project that has a key in the code and move it into a dot env file. Great work, and I'll see you next time.
